mcqs.question: What lets C# and F# code call each other directly and even inherit across languages within the same .NET project?
options: Both languages compile to the exact same Intermediate Language and run on the same CLR
The CLR automatically translates between languages at runtime
F# is actually a superset of C# syntax
Visual Studio silently converts F# projects to C# before building
mcqs.explanation: Because C# and F# both target the same IL and CLR, their compiled output is interchangeable at the runtime level — there's no cross-language translation happening, just a shared target. F# is not a C# superset, and no build step converts one language to the other.

mcqs.question: What is RyuJIT's tier 0 ("quick JIT") optimized for?
options: Maximum runtime performance regardless of compile time
Compiling as fast as possible on first call, with light instrumentation, deferring heavy optimization to tier 1
Compiling only methods marked `static`
Producing IL rather than native code
mcqs.explanation: Tier 0 exists to get a method running quickly with minimal compile-time cost while gathering call-count data; the expensive optimizations are deferred to tier 1 for methods that prove they're worth it. It isn't restricted to static methods, and it produces native code, not IL — IL is the input, not the output.

mcqs.question: How does ReadyToRun differ from full Native AOT compilation in .NET?
options: ReadyToRun ships precompiled native code alongside the IL and still allows RyuJIT to recompile hot methods later; Native AOT removes IL and the JIT entirely
ReadyToRun and Native AOT are two names for the exact same feature
ReadyToRun only works on Linux; Native AOT only works on Windows
ReadyToRun disables the garbage collector; Native AOT does not
mcqs.explanation: ReadyToRun is a hybrid — baseline native code ships alongside IL, and RyuJIT can still improve on it at runtime — while Native AOT commits fully to native code with no IL or JIT step at all. They aren't the same feature, aren't split by OS, and neither disables the GC.

mcqs.question: Which statement best characterizes the genuine architectural difference between the JVM and the CLR, rather than a superficial naming difference?
options: The CLR has no garbage collector, unlike the JVM
The CLR cannot run on Linux, unlike the JVM
IL is register-based while JVM bytecode is stack-based
AOT compilation is a more integrated, first-class part of the mainstream .NET toolchain than the JVM's separate GraalVM product
mcqs.explanation: Both runtimes are stack-based, generational-GC-backed, and cross-platform — the toolchain-level difference is that AOT (ReadyToRun/Native AOT) ships as part of mainstream .NET, whereas JVM AOT requires adopting GraalVM as a separate product. The GC, bytecode model, and Linux support claims in the other options are all factually wrong.

mcqs.question: A candidate says ".NET can't be used for a Linux-based cloud-native system because it's Windows-only." What's wrong with this claim today?
options: Nothing — the claim is still accurate for all current .NET versions
Modern .NET runs on CoreCLR, which is fully cross-platform across Linux, macOS, and Windows, with official Docker/Kubernetes support
.NET can run on Linux, but only inside a Windows virtual machine
.NET Framework was always cross-platform; only the newer .NET Core is Windows-only
mcqs.explanation: Since .NET Core (now just "​.NET", 5+), CoreCLR runs natively on Linux and macOS with first-class container support — the Windows-only constraint applied to the older .NET Framework, not modern .NET. It doesn't require a Windows VM, and the history is the reverse of what the last option claims.
